name: Sojourner
intro: Sojourner was the first wheeled robot to explore another planet. About the size of a microwave oven, it rolled from rock to rock near the Pathfinder lander in 1997. It is still out there, somewhere within about 12 meters of its lander.
whyLeft: Sojourner could only talk to Earth through the Pathfinder lander. When the lander went silent on 27 September 1997, the little rover had no way left to call home.
repurpose: Today’s rovers talk to Earth through orbiters as well as by themselves. A new radio station landed nearby could listen for Sojourner, if its solar panel still makes power.

hotspots.title: The radio antenna
hotspots.text: This antenna only reached the lander, never Earth. Once the lander stopped talking, Sojourner was cut off, even if its own parts still worked.

hotspots.title: Solar panel
hotspots.text: Sojourner ran on the sunlight falling on this small panel, less than a quarter of a square meter. Its backup batteries could not be recharged.

hotspots.title: The rock sniffer
hotspots.text: An instrument on the back, called the APXS, was pressed against rocks with nicknames like Barnacle Bill and Yogi to find out what they were made of.

photo.alt: A large pitted rock on sandy Martian ground.
photo.caption: Yogi, a rock about a meter wide, was the second rock Sojourner pressed its rock sniffer against.
photo.licenseEvidence: Commons page licence: “Public domain” (PD NASA); original source: http://mars.jpl.nasa.gov/MPF/ops/Yogi_super_res.jpg.

hotspots.title: Six little wheels
hotspots.text: Sojourner crept along at about 1 centimeter a second. In nearly three months it drove about 100 meters in all, back and forth around the lander.

hotspots.title: Front cameras
hotspots.text: Two small cameras at the front helped Sojourner spot rocks and avoid hazards. It was planned to work for a week; it kept going for almost three months.

funFact: Sojourner is named after the civil-rights hero Sojourner Truth. The name won an essay contest entered by a 12-year-old student.
